# Historical context {#sec-history}

::: {.callout-tip}
## tl;dr

Verifying other's research findings is an old endeavour, which has always been costly, and largely undervalued in recent times.
:::

The desire to check others' research is an old endeavour.
And it is not easy to do. 
Producing trustworthy scientific material is hard in any domain. 
Making that material easily accessible and verifiable complicates matters further.
And widespread access to tools that make this easier are relatively new.
Indeed, the notion of [science as practicing amateur software development](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qzVV7eEiaI) is a reasonably new possibility in the scheme of the history of science.
To make this concrete, let's look at a few moments in history.

## The emergence of the Royal Society (1600s)

The motto of the UK's [Royal Society](https://royalsociety.org/about-us/who-we-are/history/) (founded in 1662), is 'nullius in verba', which means 'take nobody's word for it'.
And indeed, in 1679, Edmond Halley travelled to Poland along with his own equipment to verify the observations made by Johannes Hevelius [@jonesHalleyAstronomer1957].
This would have been costly, in terms of time and money, but clearly underscores the value placed on verification.
But the world and science was not as widespread or as interconnected as it is now.

## The Industrial Publishing Complex (1950s onwards)

From at least the 1950s onwards, academic publishing changed dramatically in pace, scale and reach with a proliferation of journals, institutions and people working as professional academics all over the world. 
But, prior to the mass availability of the internet, sharing research materials would have remained difficult and expensive. 
And responsibilities were unclear and/or unspecified. 
For example, should the journal host all raw materials and share them upon request from others?
And who would pay for any or all of this?
As such, before the internet revolution changed things, there were legitimate practical barriers to sharing materials.

## My PhD days (2004-2007)

Even when I did my PhD, in an era when the internet was very much widespread, the idea that raw data or code would be submitted alongside a journal submission was largely unheard of in disciplines associated with psychology and neuroscience.
As an illustrative example of the times, as I prepared my very first journal article submission, I burned the raw data to a DVD (young people, see [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_disc_authoring)).
In the next meeting with my supervisors, I placed the DVD in a jiffy bag and asked: do I address this to the Editor-in-Chief and send it to the journal's mailing address?
My supervisors laughed out loud.
They then mentioned that they had heard about journals doing "data audits" before, but they didn't happen very often, and they had never been audited yet.

As a young trainee scientist, I was genuinely shocked that nobody else, other than my coauthors, would check the data.
And even then, it was certainly not routine for co-authors to go through the data and analysis steps with a fine tooth comb.
To be clear, I was very lucky to have such supportive, involved and generous supervisors. 
My observation is simply that there was a complete absence of industry standard on sharing research materials.
Even in my naive researcher state, it was clear to me that this was not how science should be conducted.
And it was also obvious that this was not how the public expected science to operate when spending taxpayer's money. 

## Towards "born open" science (2015 onwards)

As we move towards the present day, attitudes are slowly shifting.
Instead of a static pdf document being the sole "product" of a scientific project, more and more actors - spanning individuals, journals, funding agencies and learned societies - recognise that the written report is merely window dressing for everything else that supports the claims being made, such as data, code and experimental materials [@buckheitWaveLabReproducibleResearch1995; @donohoInvitationReproducibleComputational2010].
The challenge now is to build workflows that can deliver in response to this challenge.
What might that such a workflow look like, in terms of infrastructure in general and in terms of research workflows in cognitive neuroscience?
That is what this book addresses, but from the perspective of one lab.
